summary:
MoonJoy is an interactive web application designed to support the exploration and evaluation of potential landing sites near the Moon’s south pole. It combines real NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data, including Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) topography, with NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides to analyze lunar terrain, sunlight availability, and Earth visibility.

Our platform allows users to select locations on a lunar map, explore the surrounding terrain through an immersive 3D first-person view, and simulate the apparent movement of the Sun and Earth over a selected time period. It also calculates 360-degree terrain horizons, estimates communication and illumination visibility windows, and compares two candidate sites to identify periods when sunlight and direct Earth visibility overlap.

MoonJoy addresses the challenge by transforming complex scientific datasets into an accessible visual decision-support tool. This is important because limited sunlight, obstructed communication, and challenging terrain can significantly affect lunar mission planning. By helping users understand and compare these conditions, MoonJoy supports more informed preliminary site selection for future lunar exploration.
details:
MoonJoy – Project Details

Project Overview

MoonJoy is an interactive, science-based web application designed to help users explore, understand, and compare potential landing sites near the Moon's south pole. Our project transforms complex NASA scientific datasets into an accessible platform that combines realistic lunar terrain visualization, astronomical simulations, and data-driven decision support.

MoonJoy addresses a critical challenge in lunar exploration: identifying locations with favorable environmental conditions, particularly regarding sunlight availability, direct Earth visibility, and surrounding terrain.

The platform is designed for two different audiences through its Educational Mode and Professional Mode, making lunar exploration accessible to beginners while providing more detailed analytical tools for advanced users.

How Does MoonJoy Work?

MoonJoy combines real lunar topographic data from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) with astronomical calculations using NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides.

Users can select coordinates on an interactive map of the lunar south pole and explore the selected location through an immersive, first-person 3D visualization.

Using NASA elevation data, MoonJoy reconstructs the surrounding lunar terrain and calculates a 360-degree topographic horizon. This allows the application to identify mountains, crater walls, and other terrain features that may obstruct the visibility of the Sun or Earth.

Users can select a date and time interval to simulate the apparent movement of both celestial bodies. MoonJoy compares their positions with the local terrain horizon to estimate:

  • Sun Visibility: When the Sun is visible above the surrounding terrain.
  • Earth Visibility: When Earth is visible above the local horizon, indicating potential opportunities for direct communication.
  • Operational Windows: Periods during which the Sun and Earth are simultaneously visible.
  • Window Duration: The total duration and longest continuous period of favorable visibility conditions.
  • Site Comparison: Differences between two selected locations, helping users identify which site offers more favorable conditions during a specific period.

The application also provides an interactive timeline, synchronized terrain-horizon visualization, and animated Sun and Earth positions.

Educational Mode: Making Lunar Exploration Accessible

MoonJoy's Educational Mode is designed for students, educators, and people interested in space exploration who may not have a technical background.

Instead of requiring users to interpret complex scientific datasets, this mode focuses on interactive learning and visual explanations.

Users can explore the lunar surface, observe how the Sun and Earth move over time, and understand why the Moon's south pole presents unique challenges for exploration.

Educational Mode emphasizes the relationships between lunar geography, sunlight, communication, and mission planning. Through simplified explanations and visual feedback, users can discover how a small change in location can significantly affect the environmental conditions experienced by a lunar mission.

Our goal is to make real NASA data understandable, engaging, and useful for learning about space science, engineering, and planetary exploration.

Professional Mode: Data-Driven Site Analysis

MoonJoy's Professional Mode is intended for engineering students, researchers, and users who require more detailed scientific information.

This mode emphasizes quantitative results, including lunar coordinates, terrain elevation, horizon profiles, astronomical positions, visibility percentages, operational windows, and comparative performance between candidate sites.

One of its central features is the Point A vs. Point B Comparison Tool, which allows users to select two different locations and evaluate them over the same time interval.

The system compares Earth visibility, Sun visibility, simultaneous visibility periods, the number of operational windows, and the longest continuous opportunity available at each site.

This helps users identify the advantages and limitations of each location using measurable indicators rather than relying exclusively on visual inspection.

Professional Mode is designed as a preliminary analytical and decision-support tool, not as a replacement for mission-certified landing-site evaluation systems.

How MoonJoy Helps Users Make Decisions

A central objective of MoonJoy is to transform scientific measurements into information that supports informed decisions.

For example, a location may have relatively favorable terrain but experience extended periods without direct Earth visibility. Another location might provide better communication opportunities but shorter periods of sunlight.

Rather than presenting a single location as universally superior, MoonJoy allows users to compare these trade-offs.

The application helps users answer practical questions such as:

  • Which location provides more hours of sunlight during the selected period?
  • Which site offers longer potential direct communication windows with Earth?
  • When are sunlight and Earth visibility available simultaneously?
  • How long is the longest uninterrupted operational opportunity?
  • How does the surrounding terrain influence each site's visibility conditions?
  • Which location better matches the priorities of a hypothetical lunar mission?

In Educational Mode, these results help users understand the reasoning behind site selection.

In Professional Mode, the same information supports structured comparisons between alternatives, allowing users to prioritize illumination, direct Earth visibility, or simultaneous availability depending on their mission objectives.

MoonJoy does not simply display scientific data; it helps users interpret that data, compare alternatives, recognize environmental limitations, and make evidence-informed preliminary decisions.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The lunar south pole is one of the most scientifically interesting regions of the Moon, but its exploration presents considerable challenges. Low solar elevation angles, complex crater topography, and potential communication obstructions can influence the feasibility of surface operations.

MoonJoy helps users understand these challenges by connecting real scientific measurements with intuitive visualizations and comparative analysis.

The project's main benefits include:

  • Making NASA scientific datasets more accessible to students and the public.
  • Providing immersive exploration of real lunar topography.
  • Helping users understand how terrain affects sunlight and Earth visibility.
  • Supporting preliminary comparisons between potential landing sites.
  • Encouraging critical thinking through evidence-based decision-making.
  • Connecting astronomy, software development, electronics, and engineering in a single educational experience.

Our intended impact is both educational and technological.

Educationally, MoonJoy aims to inspire curiosity about lunar exploration and demonstrate how scientific data can answer practical engineering questions.

Technologically, it demonstrates how open NASA datasets can be transformed into interactive decision-support tools for preliminary mission analysis.

Technologies and Tools Used

MoonJoy was developed using scientific computing, geospatial processing, and interactive web technologies.

Programming languages and web development:

  • Python for scientific calculations and backend logic.
  • JavaScript for interactive visualization and user interactions.
  • HTML and CSS for interface design.
  • FastAPI for communication between the scientific backend and frontend.
  • Three.js for immersive 3D terrain visualization and celestial animations.

Scientific and geospatial tools:

  • NASA LOLA Digital Elevation Models for lunar topography.
  • NASA/JPL SPICE kernels and SpiceyPy for astronomical calculations.
  • NASA/JPL Horizons for additional astronomical reference data.
  • Rasterio for processing lunar elevation rasters.
  • PyProj for coordinate transformations.
  • NumPy for numerical calculations.

Development environment:

  • Visual Studio Code for programming, integration, debugging, and testing.
  • Web browsers for interacting with the application.

MoonJoy is designed to run on a conventional computer without specialized hardware.

What Makes MoonJoy Creative?

MoonJoy combines three elements that are often presented separately: scientific accuracy, immersive exploration, and decision-support analysis.

Instead of displaying only a static lunar map, MoonJoy places the user directly within a reconstructed lunar environment and allows them to observe how celestial visibility changes over time.

Its dynamic coordinate-selection system makes it possible to investigate different locations rather than relying on a single predefined landing site.

The integration of Educational and Professional Modes is another important aspect of the project's approach. Both audiences can explore the same scientific information, but with different levels of complexity and different objectives.

The A/B comparison system also transforms the experience from passive exploration into active analysis. Users can formulate hypotheses, select candidate locations, examine results, and determine which conditions better support their goals.

By connecting immersive visualization with measurable environmental conditions, MoonJoy bridges the gap between learning about the Moon and evaluating the engineering challenges of exploring it.

Factors Considered During Development

Our multidisciplinary team considered several important factors when designing MoonJoy:

Scientific reliability: We prioritized real NASA topographic and astronomical datasets over artificially generated environmental information.

Terrain and geographic accuracy: We considered lunar curvature, coordinate systems, terrain elevation, and local horizon obstruction when developing our calculations.

Dynamic environmental conditions: We designed the system to evaluate how sunlight and Earth visibility change depending on location, date, and time.

Comparison and decision-making: We incorporated measurable indicators that allow users to evaluate trade-offs between candidate landing sites.

Accessibility: We designed Educational Mode to simplify complex concepts and Professional Mode to provide more detailed analytical information.

User experience: We emphasized intuitive site selection, immersive visualization, clear results, and interactive timelines.

Computational efficiency: We incorporated reusable terrain-horizon calculations and time-based astronomical data processing to reduce unnecessary computation.

Scientific limitations: We recognize that geometric visibility does not guarantee sufficient solar power, communication-link performance, or safe landing conditions. MoonJoy is a preliminary research and educational prototype, and its scientific outputs require further validation before operational use.

Conclusion

MoonJoy transforms real NASA scientific data into an interactive experience that connects lunar exploration, education, engineering, and informed decision-making.

Through Educational Mode, the platform helps students and the public understand the environmental challenges of the Moon's south pole.

Through Professional Mode, it enables more detailed analysis and comparison of potential landing sites using quantitative visibility and operational-window indicators.

By integrating real topography, astronomical simulations, immersive 3D visualization, and comparative decision-support tools, MoonJoy demonstrates how accessible technology can help users explore not only where humanity could land on the Moon, but also why certain locations may offer better conditions for future exploration.
